bridge: Use a fictional account inventory. Do not copy passwords, recovery codes or private account information into this studio.
teaching:
### Protect the way you sign in

A unique password stops a password stolen from one service from immediately opening another. A password manager can create and store these passwords. Protect the manager itself with the safeguards its provider recommends.

Multi-factor authentication, or MFA, adds another kind of evidence at sign-in. A passkey or hardware-backed method can resist some phishing attacks better than a code that a fake website can ask you to relay. Understand the recovery method too; an attacker may try the easiest route into the account.

### Keep the device trustworthy

Install supported security updates. Use a screen lock when leaving a device, use suitable device encryption, and install software from sources you can verify. These controls protect different points; one cannot replace all the others.

### Plan for loss and mistakes

A backup is a separate recoverable copy. A synchronised folder can repeat an accidental deletion, so synchronisation alone is not always enough. Keep suitable version history or independent backups and test restoring a harmless file.

Write a simple fictional recovery plan: which account is essential, how you would regain access, and where a safe backup would come from. Keep real recovery secrets in a secure place, not in the learning notebook.

Privacy also includes collecting and sharing less information. Review which applications can access your microphone, location and files, and grant only what your actual use requires.
example:
Fictional inventory
Service        Importance   MFA       Recovery     Restore test
Demo email     high         enabled   offline kit  not applicable
Local notebook medium       device    spare copy   2026-10-29
Photo archive  medium       account   email        not tested

Do not include passwords, real recovery codes or session tokens.
explanation: The photo archive is marked not tested, so it is a recovery risk even if a backup tool reports success. The demo email has higher priority because it recovers the archive account. An offline recovery kit needs protected storage; the inventory should say where the process is documented without exposing the secret itself.
exercise: Using invented services, make three inventory rows. Copy a harmless note to a separate recovery location, remove only a disposable working copy, then restore it. Record original contents, restored contents and what failure your copy would not survive.
solution: The restored contents match. A same-disk copy does not survive disk failure. The inventory contains no authentication secrets. A good explanation links the recovery chain from one service to another.
challenge: A fictional laptop and its disk are lost. Email recovery codes existed only on that laptop; a cloud folder synchronised deletions. Identify two independent recovery weaknesses and propose a test for each.
challenge_solution: Use protected recovery material accessible without the lost laptop, and a versioned/independent backup whose retention survives deletion. Test sign-in recovery with a safe planned procedure and restore an invented file from a historical version; never disable your only working factor as a casual experiment.
